By the glorious Qur'an﴾ [Qaf 1]. ﴿Qaf﴾ is one of the letters of the alphabet of which Arabic speech is composed, and like all letters, it has no meaning in itself. It is well known that the Qur'an was revealed in the Arabic tongue, and if these letters have no meaning in the Arabic language, then they likewise have no meaning in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in terms of their intrinsic meaning (...).

This indicates that it is the speech of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy, may He be exalted. For this reason, you will hardly find a surah that begins with these alphabetic letters without the mention of the Qur'an following them.

Here Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿and by the glorious Qur'an﴾. The "wa" here is a particle of oath: Allah the Exalted swears by the Qur'an, for Allah has the right to swear by whatever He wills. His oath here by the Qur'an is an oath by His speech, and the speech of Allah is among His attributes.

The scholars—may Allah have mercy on them—have mentioned that it is permissible to swear by Allah the Exalted, or by one of His attributes. As for His signs (ayat), one should not swear by them unless the person intends by "signs" His words, such as the Noble Qur'an, the Torah, the Gospel, and the like. As for the cosmic signs, such as the sun and the moon, it is not permissible for us to swear by them; but Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, may swear by whatever He wills.

It is also glorious (majid): through it, whoever adheres to it is glorified, elevated, and made manifest. This is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Nay, it is a glorious Qur'an, in a preserved tablet﴾ [al-Buruj 21–22].

﴿By the glorious Qur'an (1). Nay, they wonder that a warner has come to them from among themselves, and the disbelievers say, "This is a strange thing."﴾ [Qaf 1–2]. Here the answer to the oath does not appear to the reader. The scholars—may Allah have mercy on them—differed regarding such cases: does it have an answer, or is its answer known from the context, or from what is sworn by? There are several opinions among the scholars. The most apparent is that we say such a construction does not require an answer to the oath, because it is known from the greatness of what is sworn to; it is as if He swore by the Qur'an to the truth of the Qur'an.

Thus the glorious Qur'an, by being glorious, is evidence that it is true and that it was sent down from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Then the oath needs no answer, since the answer is contained within the oath.

Therefore ﴿they wonder that a warner has come to them from among themselves﴾. ﴿They wonder﴾ is the wonder of astonishment and disapproval. We say this because "ajab" (wonder) is sometimes used to mean disapproval and denial, and sometimes to mean approval. The saying of 'Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her: "The Prophet, peace be upon him, liked (yu'jibuhu) to start with the right in putting on his sandals, combing his hair, purifying himself, and in all his affairs,"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (168), and Muslim (268/66).]] here the wonder means approval.

But His saying here: ﴿Nay, they wonder that a warner has come to them from among themselves﴾ means disapproval and denial.

﴿That a warner has come to them from among themselves﴾ is not something distant from them; he is one of them in lineage, nobility, and dwelling, and they know him. Yet they said, ﴿This is a strange thing.﴾

﴿When we die and become dust, that is a far return﴾ [Qaf 3]. When Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, came to them and informed them that people would be resurrected, would be recompensed and called to account, they wondered: how can this be? Can a person live again after having become decayed bones? ﴿The disbelievers say, "This is a strange thing (2). When we die and become dust..."﴾. The word ﴿idha﴾ (when) is well known to be a temporal adverb, and every adverb needs a governing element. What is its governing element? The governing element is omitted, indicated by what follows it, and the estimated meaning is: "When we die and become dust, will we return and be resurrected?!"

Then He said: ﴿That is a far return.﴾ Therefore, when reciting, it is good to pause at His saying ﴿When we die and become dust﴾, because His saying ﴿That is a far return﴾ is a new sentence (jumlah isti'nafiyyah) having no grammatical connection with what precedes it.

So ﴿idha﴾ is an adverb, and every adverb needs a governing element; where is the governing element in the verse? It is omitted; the estimated meaning is: "When we die and become dust, will we return and be resurrected?!" The interrogation here carries the sense of denial and rejection, as if they say: it is impossible that we return and are resurrected after having been dust and bones. But Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, made clear that He is able to do that. When they said ﴿That is a far return﴾, by "far" they meant impossibility; they regard it as impossible. Some of them, perhaps out of softness of speech, said ﴿That is a far return﴾. So at times they deny it absolutely, saying "This is impossible," and at other times they say "This is far-fetched."

Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah's blessings and peace be upon our Prophet Muhammad, and upon his family and companions, and those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgment.

His saying ﴿what the earth diminishes of them﴾ may indicate that the earth does not consume the whole body, and on this there is detail. As for the prophets, the earth does not consume them for as long as they remain in their graves, due to the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed Allah has forbidden the earth to consume the bodies of the prophets."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (1047), al-Nasa'i (1374), and Ibn Majah (1636) from the hadith of Aws ibn Aws.]]

As for others, the body may remain for a long period that the earth does not consume, for as long as Allah wills, and the earth may consume it. But if the earth consumes it, the 'ajb al-dhanab (the coccyx, literally "the hump of the tail") remains. The 'ajb al-dhanab is a small piece of bone at the bottom of the spine. This remains, by the permission of Allah, and the earth does not consume it. It is as if it becomes the seed of the body at its resurrection on the Day of Judgment, for from it the human being is created in his grave. When it is complete, the Trumpet is blown, and then they rise from their graves to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

﴿We know what the earth diminishes of them﴾. And if Allah the Exalted is knowing of what the earth has diminished, then He is able to return that which the earth diminished at the Resurrection.

﴿And with Us is a Book preserved﴾ [Qaf 4]: with Allah the Exalted, ﴿a Book preserved﴾, meaning one that preserves everything. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Nay, but you deny the Recompense (9). And indeed, over you are guardians (10), noble and recording (11), who know what you do﴾ [al-Infitar 9-12].

Allah the Exalted says: "Nay, but they have denied the truth when it came to them" [Qaf 5]. "Nay" (bal) here is used for a transitional shift (idrab intiqali), not a nullifying shift (idrab ibtali), because the first statement remains valid and the second is added to it. This is the difference between "bal" that nullifies (idrab ibtal) and "bal" that transitions (idrab intiqal). So "bal" is always a shift, but if it cancels the earlier statement it is called idrab ibtal, and if it does not cancel it, it is idrab intiqal, as if one has moved from one subject to another.

"They have denied the truth when it came to them": yet their hearts are certain, but their tongues deny, as Allah says about the people of Pharaoh: "And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance" [al-Naml 14].

"When it came to them" (lamma): here it means "when" (hin), so it is an adverb of time (zarf), not a particle (harf).

"So they are in a confused matter" (fa-hum fi amrin mareej): the "fa" here indicates sequence and causation. The meaning is: because they denied the truth, they are "in a confused matter", i.e., mixed up. The matter has become confused for them, and we seek refuge with Allah. This is like Allah's saying: "And We turn their hearts and their sights away, as they did not believe in it the first time, and We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly" [al-An'am 110], meaning: because they did not believe in it the first time. Those who denied, when they denied, came to be in a confused matter; the affair became ambiguous to them, and they vacillated about their situation.

Likewise, every person who rejects the truth the first time should know that he will be tested with doubt and suspicion in accepting the truth in the future.

Therefore, we must, from the moment we hear that something is true, say: "We hear and we obey", unlike some people today. You tell one of them: "The Messenger commanded this," and he says: "Fine, is the command obligatory or recommended?" Glory be to Allah! Do what he commanded you, whether it is obligatory or recommended.

If you hesitate, because the meaning of your question, "Is it obligatory or recommended?", is: if it is recommended I am free of it, and if it is obligatory I will do it, this is a mistake. Say: "We hear and we obey." Then, if a violation occurs, the question of whether it is obligatory or recommended may be worthwhile; but before that, no.

Someone may say: "I ask whether it is obligatory or recommended because there is a difference between the obligatory and the recommended, and which of them is more beloved to Allah? The obligatory is more beloved to Allah, so I do it so that if I believe it is obligatory I receive the reward of an obligation, and if I believe it is a sunnah I receive the reward of a sunnah."

We say: Yes, this is fine, but the reward of submitting to the truth the first time, and with ease, without asking, is better than your believing it to be obligatory or recommended. If Allah has made it obligatory upon you, He rewards you with the reward of an obligation; and if you do not know, then submission and complete submission is far better than my believing this to be obligatory or recommended.

The Mighty and Majestic says: "So they are in a confused matter" [Qaf 5], then He says: "Have they not looked at the sky above them?" [Qaf 6]. He uses the cosmic signs as evidence for the validity of the legislative signs. Its discussion, God willing, will come in the next session (...).

Now we have reached His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Indeed, We know what the earth diminishes of them, and with Us is a preserved Record. But they have denied the truth when it came to them, so they are in a confused state.﴾ Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them, how We constructed it and adorned it, and it has no cracks?﴾ [Qaf 6]. The interrogative here is for reproach. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, rebukes them: Why did they not look into this? Why did they not look at the sky and at its wonders of power, which indicate that Allah the Exalted is able to bring the dead back to life, something these deniers rejected?

His saying: ﴿Have they not looked at the sky﴾ includes both sight of the eye (naẓar al-baṣar) and sight of insight (naẓar al-baṣīrah). Sight of the eye is by the eye, and sight of insight is by the heart, and it is reflection (tafakkur).

His saying: ﴿at the sky above them, how We constructed it﴾ — someone may say: the word ﴿above them﴾ has no benefit, since it is well known that the sky is above. But we say: the explicit statement that it is above them points to the greatness of this sky, and that, despite its height, elevation, vastness and magnificence, it demonstrates the perfection of its Creator and His power, exalted is He.

﴿how We constructed it﴾: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, built it with strength, and made it strong. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We constructed above you seven strong [heavens]﴾ [An-Naba' 12], meaning strong. And He, exalted, said: ﴿And the sky — We constructed it with might﴾, meaning with strength, ﴿and indeed, We are its expanders﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat 47].

We do not know how Allah, Mighty and Majestic, constructed this building, but we know that He created the heavens and the earth in six days: He created the earth in four, and the heavens in two days, as He, exalted, said: ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens in two days﴾ [Fussilat 12].

His saying: ﴿and We adorned it﴾ means: We made its appearance beautiful by what Allah the Exalted created in it of great, shining stars, orderly in their courses. Regarding these stars, Qatadah, may Allah have mercy on him, who is among the great Successors (a'immat al-tabi'in), said, may Allah have mercy on him: Allah created these stars for three purposes: as an adornment for the sky, as signs by which one is guided, and as missiles against the devils. Whoever seeks in them anything other than this has lost his share and burdened himself with what he has no knowledge of.[[Narrated by al-Tabari in his Tafsir (23/123).]] He is referring to what the astrologers (al-munajjimun) claim, deducing earthly events from the movements of these stars, to the extent that they base a person's happiness and misery on them. For example, they say: if he is born under such-and-such a star, he is happy, and if he is born under such-and-such a star, he is wretched. This has no basis; I mean, the movements of the stars in the sky have no effect on what happens on earth.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿and it has no cracks﴾, meaning: there are no cracks in the sky, that is, no rifts or splits; rather it is constructed, firm and strong.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 50, verse 7:

﴿And the earth—We spread it out and cast into it firm mountains and caused to grow in it every beautiful pair﴾ [Qaf 50:7]. These are three matters.

First: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, spread out the earth, even though it is very small compared to the heavens. Yet it is spread out for the creatures and laid flat for them, as the Most High said: ﴿And at the earth, how it has been spread out?﴾ [al-Ghashiyah 88:20].

Second: ﴿We cast into it firm mountains﴾, meaning mountains that are fixed and that the winds cannot shake. They are "rasiyah" (firmly set), and likewise they serve as anchors (mursiyah) for the earth.

﴿And caused to grow in it every beautiful pair﴾, meaning every kind that is pleasing to the one who looks at it. Here "zawj" (pair) means kind or type. What grows in the earth consists of many varied kinds. You may see a small patch of earth containing types of these kinds that differ in their colors, differ in their sizes, and differ in their textures, some hard and some soft, along with other great differences. They even differ in taste when they bear fruit, as the Most High said: ﴿And We make some of them exceed others in food﴾ [ar-Ra'd 13:4]. So who is able to do this?

* Student: Able to do what?

* Shaykh: To create these things within them, every beautiful pair, although they are in one place, watered with one water, and the earth is one. The answer is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Who else is able to do this? You come upon a land covered with plants, in which Allah the Most High has made grow various kinds of vegetation, and you are amazed. You see that this one's flower is yellow, that one's is white, another's is violet, one is open, another is closed, along with other magnificent signs. This is the greatest proof that Allah is able to bring the dead back to life, which these deniers of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rejected, saying: ﴿When we have died and become dust—that is a far return﴾ [Qaf 50:3]. So the One who is able to create these great creatures is able to bring the dead back to life.

Then it is said: Who created man? It is Allah. And the re-creation is easier than the initial creation, as the Most High said: ﴿And it is He who begins creation and then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ [ar-Rum 30:27]. So if you, O polytheists, acknowledge that Allah is the Creator, and that He is the One who created you and brought you into existence, then why do you deny that Allah can return you, when His command, whenever He wills something, is only to say to it, "Be," and it is?

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿A insight and a reminder for every servant who turns back in repentance﴾ [Qaf 8]. That is, Allah the Exalted has urged us to look at the heavens and the earth and at what happens within them.

﴿Insight﴾ means: for the sake of insight and reminder. The scholars said: the difference between insight (tabsirah) and reminder (dhikra) is that insight is continuous, while reminder is at the time of forgetfulness. So these signs remind you when you forget, and give you insight when you are ignorant. It is also said that the difference between them is that insight is the opposite of ignorance (jahl), and reminder is the opposite of forgetfulness (nisyan). Both statements are true.

The point is that when you look at the heavens and the earth and what is in them, of what Allah the Mighty and Majestic has placed there, such as plants, you will gain insight with your heart, and you will also be reminded when you forget. But for whom is this insight and reminder? ﴿For every servant who turns back in repentance﴾. It is not for every person. How often do the disbelievers look at the signs, yet ﴿signs and warnings avail not a people who do not believe﴾ [Yunus 101]. Rather, the ones who benefit from them are ﴿every servant who turns back in repentance﴾, that is, one who returns often to Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

Then the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿And We send down from the sky blessed water﴾ [Qaf 9]. We will stop here until the next lesson, or the next meeting, God willing (...).

We begin this session with what is easy to say about verses from Surah Qaf, namely God's words: ﴿And We sent down from the sky blessed water, and We caused to grow thereby gardens and grain for harvest, and tall date palms with ranged spathes﴾ [Qaf 9–11].

He says: ﴿We sent down﴾ (nazzalna), because rain falls little by little. It is sometimes expressed with (anzala), because by it the valleys and watercourses flow.

His words ﴿from the sky﴾ mean from the height, because this rain descends from the clouds and not from the sky that is the protected ceiling. The evidence is His words: ﴿and the clouds subjected between the sky and the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah 164]. So it descends from above. The wisdom in its descent from above is that it reaches the peaks of mountains, the pasture of camels, the plains and the valleys. If it came flowing (sayhan) along the ground, it would not reach the peaks of the mountains, but Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made it come from above.

His words ﴿blessed water﴾: among its blessings is that Allah causes by it ﴿gardens and grain for harvest﴾. The jannat (gardens) are the many-treed orchards, and orchards with many trees are called jannat because they conceal (tujinn), that is, they cover what is beneath them. Every orchard with trees intertwined with one another is called a jannah.

As for His words ﴿grain for harvest﴾, He means the crops that are reaped. Here Allah mentioned trees and crops: from trees fruit is plucked, and from crops grain is harvested.

﴿And the date palms with ranged spathes﴾ [Qaf 10]: Allah singled out the date palm because it is the noblest of trees. For this reason the believer was compared to it, when the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Among the trees there is one whose likeness is that of the believer." Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: People began to speculate about the trees of the desert (bawadi), each saying, "It is such-and-such tree." Ibn 'Umar said: It came into my heart that it is the palm tree, but I was the youngest of the people. (He meant that he was shy to speak, being the youngest.) So the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is the palm tree."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (61) and Muslim (2811/63).]] This is the tree mentioned in the words of Allah: ﴿Have you not considered how Allah presents a parable: a good word like a good tree, whose root is firmly fixed and whose branches are in the sky﴾ [Ibrahim 24]. For this reason He singled it out here, saying: ﴿and the date palms with ranged spathes﴾, meaning tall (ba'iqat), lofty.

﴿It has ranged spathes (tal'un nadid)﴾, meaning arranged in order (mandud). The spathe (tal') on its strands is found arranged in the finest order, and yet these fruits are carried on a thin, supple strand, though it may sometimes bear more than thirty fruits or even more.

﴿It has ranged spathes﴾ [Qaf 10] ﴿a provision for the servants﴾ [Qaf 11]: meaning, We did that. We sent down water from the sky, ﴿and caused to grow thereby gardens and grain for harvest, and the date palms with ranged spathes﴾, We did that as ﴿a provision for the servants﴾, meaning a gift and bounty for the servants. Here "the servants" includes both believing servants and disbelieving servants, because the disbeliever is a servant of Allah, as Allah said: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam 93]. The intended meaning here is universal, decreed servitude (al-'ubudiyyah al-kawniyyah al-qadariyyah). As for legal servitude (al-'ubudiyyah al-shar'iyyah), one is not a servant of Allah in that sense except the one who complies with His command, avoids His prohibition, and affirms His report.

So ﴿for the servants﴾ includes disbelievers and believers.

﴿And We revived thereby a dead land﴾ [Qaf 11]: ﴿We revived thereby﴾, meaning by the water We sent down from the sky, ﴿a dead land﴾. ﴿a land﴾ (baldah) is feminine in wording but masculine in meaning, so it is correct to describe it with a masculine adjective: ﴿a dead land﴾, meaning a dead land, which He revived with this water sent down from the sky. How is its reviving? You find the earth lifeless and barren, with no plant in it. When Allah sends down rain, it swells with plants, turns green and flourishes. This is life after death.

﴿Thus is the emergence﴾ [Qaf 11]: meaning, like that reviving is the emergence of people from their graves before Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Allah mentioned the emergence only because some of Allah's servants denied it. ﴿Those who disbelieved claim that they will never be resurrected﴾ [al-Taghabun 7]. Their argument was that they said: ﴿Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾ [Ya-Sin 78]: how can bones be revived after they have rotted and become dust? This seemed to them outlandish and remote. But Allah, glorified and exalted, made clear that it is not remote, and that just as they see the dead earth, rain descends upon it and it comes to life, so the One who is able to revive the earth after its death by sending down rain is able to revive the dead after their death. This is a clear and evident analogy (qiyas jali).

This is the commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 50, verses 12–14:

﴿Thus will be the Resurrection (11). The people of Noah, the companions of the Rass (the well), and Thamud denied before them (12), and 'Ad, Pharaoh, and the brothers of Lot (13), and the companions of the Thicket, and the people of Tubba' (14).﴾ God mentioned these deniers for two benefits. The first benefit: to console the Messenger ﷺ, by telling him that he is not the first messenger to be denied, for messengers before him were denied as well, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you﴾ [Fussilat 43]. It was said that he was a poet, and it was said that he was a madman, and it was said that he was a soothsayer. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Likewise, there came not to those before them any messenger except that they said, "A magician or a madman!"﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 52].

This is the benefit of mentioning the stories of past nations, and it is the consolation of the Prophet ﷺ; for when a person sees another afflicted with a calamity like his own, he is without doubt consoled, and the calamity becomes easier for him to bear.

The second benefit: a warning to those who deny the Messenger ﷺ. For this reason He said at the end of what He mentioned: ﴿Each one denied the messengers, so My warning was realized﴾, meaning: the warning of Allah of punishment was justly due upon them. Allah the Mighty and Majestic has said: ﴿So We seized each one for his sin﴾ [al-'Ankabut 40], meaning: each one of these nations was recompensed with the like of his sin and punished with the like of his sin. For example: ﴿The people of Noah denied before them, and the companions of the Rass, and Thamud﴾. The people of Noah denied Noah, peace be upon him, and he remained among them for a thousand years less fifty years, that is, nine hundred and fifty years, calling them to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, but they gained nothing from that. Whenever he called them that God might forgive them, ﴿they put their fingers in their ears and covered themselves with their garments﴾: they covered themselves, ﴿and persisted and were excessively arrogant﴾ [Nuh 7]. He remained among them for this period, and Allah the Exalted said at the end: ﴿And none believed with him except a few﴾ [Hud 40].

﴿The people of Noah denied before them, and the companions of the Rass, and Thamud﴾. The companions of the Rass were a people whose prophet came to them, but they killed him at the Rass, which is a well; that is, they dug a well and buried him. This is one opinion. The second opinion: the companions of the Rass means a people living around a water source, who were not of great number, and yet they denied their messenger.

Thamud were the people of Salih in the well-known land of al-Hijr. They denied Salih and said: ﴿Bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the messengers﴾ [al-A'raf 77]. This was a challenge. So what did Allah do to them? He sent upon them a blast and an earthquake, and ﴿they became in their homes fallen prostrate﴾ [Hud 67].

﴿And 'Ad﴾ [Qaf 13]. Likewise, 'Ad: Allah sent Hud to them, and they denied him, so Allah destroyed them with the wind. He sent upon them ﴿the barren wind, which left nothing it came upon without making it like rotted remains﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 41–42].

They used to boast of their strength, saying: ﴿Who is mightier than us in strength?﴾ [Fussilat 15]. So Allah the Mighty and Majestic showed them His power and destroyed them with a gentle wind that has no visible body; yet it utterly destroyed them.

﴿And Pharaoh﴾, to whom Allah sent His prophet Moses, peace be upon him. He was known for tyranny, obstinacy and arrogance, to the extent that he made his people feeble-minded and said to them that he was a lord. He said: ﴿I am your lord, the Most High﴾ [an-Nazi'at 24], and they obeyed him. Moses, peace be upon him, came to them with clear signs, but they denied. Allah the Exalted showed them a sign that opposed what Moses had brought, and they boasted of it: it was magic. They gathered all the sorcerers in Egypt for Moses, peace be upon him, and they assembled and threw down their ropes and staves, and cast magic upon them, so the people saw these ropes and staves as if they were serpents and snakes, and the people were terrified, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They terrified the people and brought a great magic﴾ [al-A'raf 116]. So much so that Moses, peace be upon him, sensed fear within himself, meaning he saw that all the air around him was serpents wanting to devour whatever faced them. Allah the Exalted revealed to Moses: ﴿Throw down your staff﴾ [al-A'raf 117]. He threw down the staff, and it swallowed all these serpents. This was one of the signs of Allah, since the snake, as is known, is not that large; yet it devoured these ropes and staves, which vanished like vapor. The sorcerers saw a matter that amazed them, and they could not restrain themselves except to believe, and with complete faith: ﴿the sorcerers were cast down prostrating﴾.

Consider His saying: ﴿The sorcerers were cast down prostrating﴾ [al-A'raf 120]. He did not say "they prostrated," as if something compelled them to prostrate, as if they prostrated involuntarily, because of the strength of the great sign they had seen. Yet despite this clear sign manifesting the truthfulness of Moses, peace be upon him, Pharaoh did not believe, and said: ﴿Indeed, these are a small band, and indeed they have enraged us﴾ [ash-Shu'ara' 54–55]. So he resolved to attack Moses and the believers with him. Allah commanded Moses to leave Egypt toward the east, toward the Red Sea. He obeyed Allah's command and left Egypt in that direction. Pharaoh followed them with his armies in rage, wanting to finish off Moses and his people. When they reached the sea, the people of Moses said to him: ﴿Indeed, we are overtaken﴾ [ash-Shu'ara' 61]. He said: ﴿No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me﴾ [ash-Shu'ara' 62]. Allah revealed to him that he should strike the sea with his staff, a sea whose breadth spans long distances. He struck the sea and it parted into twelve paths, and the pieces of water became like mountains. These paths, which had been moist water and slippery mud, became dry road in an instant by Allah's permission. Moses and his people entered and crossed from Africa to Asia through the sea. When they had all completed their passage to the eastern side, Pharaoh and his people entered, and when they had all entered, Allah commanded the sea and it closed over them.

When Pharaoh faced drowning, he declared: ﴿I believe that there is no deity except the one in whom the Children of Israel believe﴾ [Yunus 90]. Consider that he did not say "I believe in Allah"; he said "I believe in that in which the Children of Israel believe." Why? As self-humiliation, since he had been denying the Children of Israel and attacking them, and now at death he acknowledged that he was their follower, one of their tails, meaning that he walked behind them. But what was said to him? ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters﴾ [Yunus 91]. His repentance was not accepted, because he repented only when death was present, and repentance after the presence of death does not benefit, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now"﴾ [an-Nisa' 18]. Repentance does not benefit when death is present. We ask Allah the Exalted to grant us and you repentance before death.

But Allah said: ﴿So today We will save you in your body that you may be a sign to those after you﴾ [Yunus 92]. "In your body," meaning not in your spirit: the spirit had departed from the body, but the body remained floating on the water. Why? Allah explained the wisdom: ﴿that you may be a sign to those after you﴾ [Yunus 92]. Allah sent them a messenger, and they denied him and did not submit to him. So the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Each one denied the messengers, so My warning was realized﴾, meaning that these nations whose narratives Allah has related—indeed, Allah pointed to all their stories—each denied the messengers, so the promise of Allah of His punishment and retribution was justly due upon them, may Allah protect us. We ask Allah to grant us and you protection and well-being; indeed, He is over all things competent (...).

Let us begin this session with what is easy of discussion concerning the surah ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an﴾.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Were We then wearied by the first creation? Nay, but they are in confusion about a new creation﴾ [Qaf 15]. The interrogative here is for negation. ('Iyina) means "we became weary." The first creation is the beginning of creatures. The meaning is: Have We become incapable of originating creation, that We would be incapable of recreating it? It is well known that the answer is no, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Do they not see that Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and was not wearied by their creation, is able to give life to the dead? Yes, indeed; He is over all things competent﴾ [al-Ahqaf 33]. That is, He was not tired by that. So if He, glorified and exalted, was not wearied by the first creation, then recreating creation is easier than originating it, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And it is He who originates creation and then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ [ar-Rum 27]. This is a rational argument intended to persuade those who deny the recreation of creation. Those who disbelieved claimed that they would never be resurrected, and that there is no resurrection, and they denied this. They argued for it with a very weak proof, saying: ﴿Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾ [Ya-Sin 78]. So Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say, "He will give them life who produced them the first time, and He is Knowing of every creation"﴾ [Ya-Sin 79]. Then he went on to cite the rational proofs indicating that Allah, the Exalted, is able to give life to bones when they are decayed.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Nay, but they are in confusion about a new creation﴾ [Qaf 15]. That is: they acknowledge that We were not wearied by the first creation and that We brought it into existence, but ﴿they are in confusion about a new creation﴾. For this reason the transition (idrab) is apt here, where He said: ﴿Nay, but they﴾, meaning that this is a wonder regarding their condition: how do they affirm the origin of creation and then deny resurrection after death? ﴿Nay, but they are in confusion﴾, that is, in doubt and hesitation, ﴿in confusion about a new creation﴾, which is the recreation of creation.

Now I ask you: Is the one who is able to originate creation also able to recreate it, and more so? The answer is yes, and this is a rational proof that no person can escape.

Then the Exalted said, in proof of His power to resurrect: ﴿And We have certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him﴾ [Qaf 16]. That is, We began his creation, brought him into existence, and gave him intellect, hearing, sight, thought, and inner speech of the soul.

﴿And We know what his soul whispers to him﴾: that is, We know what his soul whispers to him, i.e., what his soul speaks to him within himself without uttering it. Allah the Exalted knows it, and indeed Allah knows what his soul will whisper to him in the future, whereas the human being himself does not know what his soul will whisper to him in the future.

Now consider: what a person's soul whispers to him in the present, the person knows, does he not? And Allah knows it too. We say: rather, Allah knows what his soul will whisper in the future, while the person does not know. That is, Allah knows what your soul will whisper to you tomorrow and the day after, and until you die, while you do not know.

If Allah knows what the soul whispers, what does this knowledge require of us? It requires us to be mindful of Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, and not to let our souls speak of what angers Him and what He dislikes. All the talk of our souls should be of what pleases Him, because He knows it. Is it not fitting for us to be ashamed before our Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, that our souls whisper what He does not approve?

The reason is that the nearness of Allah is a lofty attribute that is not fitting to be general to every human being; for if we said that the intended meaning is the nearness of Allah's Essence, He would be near to the disbeliever just as He is near to the believer. Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 50, verse 18:

﴿Not a word does he utter but that with him is a watcher ready [to record].﴾ [Qaf: 18], ﴿Not a word does he utter﴾: ﴿مَا﴾ (ma) is a negative particle, and ﴿قَوْلٍ﴾ (qawl, "word") is in the genitive case due to the extra (za'ida) preposition ﴿مِنْ﴾ (min), which is grammatically superfluous (ziyada i'rab) but semantically meaningful (mufida ma'na). Its original form without the addition would be: ma yalfizu qawlan. However, prepositions sometimes appear as extra in grammatical analysis while still conveying the meaning of emphasis. For this reason, when a negated noun is accompanied by the extra ﴿مِنْ﴾ or the extra ﴿بِ﴾ (ba'), the negation is more emphatic in generality than a bare negation without the extra preposition, as in the verse: ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat: 46]. 

﴿Not a word does he utter﴾: if we consider ﴿مِنْ﴾ to be grammatically extra but semantically meaningful, what is its semantic function? It is the emphasis on generality: any word a person utters ﴿with him is a watcher ready﴾. Glory be to God! ﴿رَقِيبٌ﴾ (raqib, "watcher") is one who observes night and day, never separating from the person; ﴿عَتِيدٌ﴾ ('atid, "ready") means present; he cannot be absent and delegate someone else. He sits, observing, present, and nothing escapes him. ﴿مِنْ قَوْلٍ﴾: which word? Every word; because this ﴿مِنْ﴾ is extra, and ﴿قَوْلٍ﴾ is an indefinite noun in a negative context, so it is general: any word he says.

The apparent meaning of the noble verse is that whatever the word, it is recorded, whether good, evil, or idle talk. However, one is held accountable only for what is good or evil, and recording does not necessarily mean that the person will be held accountable for it. This is the apparent meaning of the wording, and it is one of the two opinions of the scholars.

Among the scholars are those who say that only good deeds and evil deeds are recorded; idle talk is not recorded. Which of the two opinions is preferable? The first is preferable, namely the generality. As for the outcome, it is one: even according to the view that the recorder writes everything, they say that one is held accountable only for good and evil deeds.

However, our saying in terms of generality is what conforms to the apparent meaning of the verse, and it is also the evidence that the two angels neither err nor omit anything, which indicates the completeness of their care for what a person utters.

Accordingly, brothers, we must guard our tongues with the utmost caution, for how many slips of the tongue have brought about ruin, may God protect us. Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him) said concerning the man who said: "By Allah, Allah will not forgive so-and-so," whereupon Allah said: "Who is this who swears by Me that I will not forgive so-and-so? I have forgiven him and nullified your deeds," and he said: "He spoke a word that ruined his worldly life and his Hereafter."[[Recorded by Muslim (2621/137) from Jundub ibn 'Abd Allah al-Bajali, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man said: 'By Allah, Allah will not forgive so-and-so,' and Allah the Exalted said: 'Who is this who swears by Me that I will not forgive so-and-so? Indeed I have forgiven so-and-so and nullified your deeds.'" As for the statement of Abu Hurayra at the end of the hadith, it is recorded by Abu Dawud (4901) from his narration with the wording: "By the One in whose hand is my soul, he spoke a word that ruined his worldly life and his Hereafter."]] We ask Allah for well-being.

Beware of your tongue lest you speak and be tested;
Indeed, affliction is entrusted to speech.

Beware the afflictions of the tongue. The Prophet (ﷺ) made guarding the tongue the foundation of the whole matter. He said to Mu'adh ibn Jabal: "Shall I not direct you to the foundation of all that?" I said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He took hold of his own tongue and said: "Restrain this upon yourself," meaning do not let it loose, do not speak. "He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, will we be held accountable for what we say?' He said to him: 'May your mother be bereft of you, O Mu'adh! Do people get thrown on their faces, or on their noses, into the Fire except for the harvest of their tongues?'"[[Recorded by al-Tirmidhi (2616) and Ibn Majah (3973).]] Therefore the believer must guard his tongue, for it is a great affliction.

For this reason the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or remain silent."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6018) and Muslim (47/75) from the hadith of Abu Hurayra.]]

From this we know that silence is preferable to speech, because a person may not know whether his speech is good or evil.

Furthermore, I say to you: a word, once you utter it and it leaves your mouth, is like a bullet you fire at your child. Can you stop the bullet once it has left the barrel of the rifle? No, it has already been released; it corrupts or it benefits. So too is the word. The wise person restrains his tongue and speaks only good, and good is either in the speaker himself or in others. That is, speech may not be good in itself, yet it is good in terms of its effects. A person may speak idle words in a gathering—words that are neither commanding good nor forbidding evil, nor sin and burden—but he speaks in order to open the door for those present, because sometimes awe takes hold of the gathering and no one speaks, so people remain as though in distress. So he speaks to open the door for people, their hearts are relieved, and an exchange of words takes place that may be beneficial. We say: this speech by which he opened the door of conversation and removed the distress from people—is it good in itself or good for something else? It is good for something else. This falls, God willing, under the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or remain silent."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6018) and Muslim (47/75) from the hadith of Abu Hurayra.]]

We ask Allah to grant us and you the guarding of our tongues and limbs from what displeases Him, and to employ them in what pleases Him; indeed He is capable of all things (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 50, verse 19:

We begin this session with a discussion of what is easy to explain from the tafsir of Surah Qaf.

The verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the agony of death will come in truth. That is what you were trying to avoid.﴾ (19) ﴿And the Horn will be blown. That is the Day of the Promised Punishment.﴾ (20) ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness.﴾ (21) [Qaf 19-21].

﴿The agony of death will come﴾. Here, sakrah (agony, overwhelming stupor) means the covering of the intellect, like fainting and the like. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, death has agonies" [Reported by al-Bukhari (4449) from the hadith of 'A'ishah]. On this basis, His saying "sakrat al-mawt" (the agony of death) is a singular noun in the construct state, so it includes one agony or more.

His saying "bil-haqq" (in truth) means that death is true, as in the hadith: "Death is true, Paradise is true, and the Fire is true" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1120) and Muslim (769 / 199) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, and its wording is: "You are the Truth, Your promise is true, Your meeting is true, Your word is true, Paradise is true, and the Fire is true"]. So it comes with truth, and it also comes with the certainty of truth (haqq al-yaqin), for at the time of death a person witnesses what he was threatened with and what he was promised, because if he is a believer he is given the good news of Paradise, and if he is a disbeliever he is given the good news of the Fire, may Allah protect us and you from it.

﴿That﴾, i.e., death, ﴿is what you were trying to avoid﴾. The exegetes differed concerning "mā": is it negation, so the meaning is: that from which you cannot escape and from which you cannot be free; or is it a relative pronoun, so the meaning is: that which you were trying to avoid, but there is no escape from it.

According to the first view, the meaning of the verse is: that which you cannot avoid, rather it is inevitable, and Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: Indeed, the death from which you flee will surely meet you﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 8].

Reflect, my brother, on: ﴿Say: Indeed, the death from which you flee will surely meet you﴾; He did not say "will overtake you." Consider a thing you flee from while it is meeting you. Indeed, your fleeing from it means your approaching it in reality; if you were fleeing from something that was confronting you, then the more you hasten in running, the more you hasten to meet it. For this reason He said: ﴿it will surely meet you﴾. In the second verse: ﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you should be in towers built up high﴾ [an-Nisa' 78]; because He mentioned in this second verse that a person, however fortified he may be, death will overtake him in every case.

Here He says: ﴿That is what you were trying to avoid﴾ [Qaf 19], meaning: that from which there is no escape for you.

The second meaning of "mā" is that it is a relative pronoun, i.e., that which you were trying to avoid and flee from during your life has reached you and overtaken you.

In any case, the verse contains a warning against neglecting righteous deeds and being lax in repentance, and that a person must hasten, because he does not know when death will come to him.

[Qur'an 50:20] Then He said: ﴿And the Horn will be blown. That is the Day of the Threat.﴾ The one who blows the Horn (al-Sur) is an angel whom Allah the Exalted has appointed for this task, named Israfil. The blowing of the Horn occurs in two blasts. The first is the blast of terror (nafkhat al-sa'q): there will be a dread that precedes it, and then swooning. The second is the blast of resurrection (nafkhat al-ba'th). Between them is forty. Abu Hurayra, the narrator of the hadith, was asked: "What is meant by the forty?" He said: "Abaytu" (ابيت), meaning: I do not know what is meant by the forty that the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned.[[Agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh); al-Bukhari (4814), and Muslim (2955 / 141).]]

The point is that what is meant by His words here, ﴿The Horn will be blown﴾, is the second blast, as evidenced by His words ﴿That is the Day of the Threat﴾. This means that by this blast the Day of Resurrection, which is the Day of the Threat, comes into being.

If someone says: The Day of Resurrection is a day of threat and a day of promise. The threat is for whom? For the disbelievers. The promise is for the believers. Why, then, did Allah the Exalted mention here the threat without the promise? Because the entire surah begins with the denial of the deniers of the Messenger (peace be upon him), so it was fitting that the aspect of threat predominate in it: ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an (1). Nay, they wonder that a warner from among themselves has come to them﴾ [Qaf 1-2], and so on to the end. Thus it was wise to mention the threat without the promise. Nevertheless, Allah the Exalted did mention the people of Paradise later on, because the Qur'an is ﴿mathani﴾ (oft-repeated).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 50, verse 21:

﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness.﴾ [Qaf: 21] ﴿Came﴾ means: on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿Every soul﴾, i.e., every person, every human being. It may also mean: every soul among the children of Adam and also among the jinn who are bound by the sharia (divine law). For if we look at the context, which is His saying: ﴿And We have certainly created man and We know what his own self whispers to him﴾ and so on, we say that the word "soul" here refers to the soul of man. And if we look at the fact that the sharia binds the jinn just as it binds mankind, and that the jinn will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection, with their believers entering Paradise and their disbelievers entering the Fire, we say that this is general. And Allah knows best what He intended.

﴿With it a driver﴾ who drives it, ﴿and a witness﴾ who testifies against it for what it did. For these angels, peace be upon them, have been appointed to record the deeds of the children of Adam, good and bad, and as has already been mentioned, they record everything: the good, the bad, and the idle talk. But a person is only held to account for the good or the bad.

Ibn 'Uthaymin said, may Allah have mercy on him: Then Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿You were certainly heedless of this﴾ [Qaf 22]. To whom does the address ﴿you﴾ refer? It refers to the human being. In this verse there is what is called *iltifāt* (the shift in grammatical person within a passage). *Iltifāt* means that a speaker moves in his discourse from second person (*khiṭāb*, direct address) to third person (*ghaybah*, absence), or from third person to second person, or from first person to third person. The point is that the pronouns change. The benefit of this is that it draws the listener's attention, since when speech follows one pattern and then suddenly changes, the listener is alert.

Consider His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah had certainly taken the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾, and after it: ﴿And We raised among them twelve leaders﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 12]. He did not say "and He raised," but shifted to "We."

Consider also al-Fatihah, which we recite every day in every rak'ah of our prayers: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. The Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Sovereign of the Day of Recompense﴾ [al-Fatihah 2–4]. After it comes ﴿It is You we worship﴾ [al-Fatihah 5], and He did not say *iyyāhu na'budu* (the third-person form, "It is Him we worship"). The context of the verses is third person, ﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾, which is not addressed to a listener; one would not say, "All praise is due to You, O Lord."

So the point is that *iltifāt* is a feature of the Arabic language, and its benefit is to draw the listener's attention to what is being said to him.

As for ﴿You were certainly heedless of this﴾: as you know, the sentence here is emphasized by three emphatic particles. ﴿Certainly (*laqad*)﴾ and the verb *kunta* (you were), a construction that occurs very frequently in the Qur'an, as in *laqad kunta*, *laqad kāna*, *laqad jā'a*. The scholars say that this sentence is emphasized by three emphatics: the first is the oath, the second is the *lām* (the emphatic lām), and the third is *qad*. The implied meaning is: "By Allah, you were certainly heedless of this."

Here we raise a question: Is not the news of Allah, the Exalted, true and sincere, whether it is emphasized or not? Yes, undoubtedly. But since the Qur'an was revealed in the clear Arabic tongue, emphasis must occur where it is appropriate and be absent where it is not appropriate, because the aim is for this Qur'an to be at the highest level of eloquence.

﴿You were﴾, i.e., O human being, ﴿heedless of this﴾, i.e., you were heedless of this Day, forgetful in the world as if you had been created for it alone.

﴿So We have removed from you your covering﴾, meaning: on this Day the covering is lifted, the hidden is made manifest, and everything becomes clear.

We ask Allah, the Exalted, to make our end and our final outcome good, both for us and for you, and to gather us with those whom Allah has blessed: the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous (...).

* Student: Singular.

You have understood the examples and evidence for what we have mentioned.

Let us begin this session, as is our custom, with the explanation of the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, which is the most noble, the best, and the most beneficial speech for the hearts. This is part of Allah's care for you, O human being, that He has appointed these angels over you, who know what you do and write it down, adding nothing to it and taking nothing away from it.

He says: ﴿This is what is ready with me﴾, meaning: present, and ready for the person.

Then it is said: ﴿Cast into Hell every stubborn disbeliever﴾ [Qaf 24]. The phrase ﴿Cast into Hell﴾ may cause difficulty for the student of knowledge, because He said: ﴿And his companion will say, "This is what is ready with me,"﴾. Is "companion" singular or dual?

* Student: Singular.

* The Shaykh: Singular. Yet here ﴿Cast﴾ contains the dual ending (alif of duality). So how is it correct to address a single one with the address of two? The exegetes differed in answering this. ﴿every stubborn disbeliever (24), obstructer of good, transgressor, doubter (25), who has set up with Allah another god﴾ [Qaf 24–26]. It may be said that it is an intensive form, because this disbeliever has committed many kinds of disbelief, and when the kinds are gathered they become many. It may also be said that this form is not intensive but a form of attribution (sigha nisba), as one says najjar (carpenter) and haddad (blacksmith) and similar ones who are attributed to a craft, so the meaning is "disbeliever," i.e., one who is a disbeliever, but disbelief has become firmly rooted in his heart, and we seek refuge in Allah.

The third attribute: ﴿obstructer of good (mannaʿ lil-khayr)﴾ means he prevents good: he prevents calling to Allah, prevents spending his wealth in what pleases Allah, and prevents every good, because the word ﴿good﴾ is general and includes every good. And ﴿mannaʿ﴾ seems to seek out every good in order to prevent it, so this form is intensive.

Consider, for example, the disbelievers of Quraysh: what did they do with the Messenger? Did they prevent him from good or not? They prevented him. Did they attack him? Yes, they attacked him.

If this phrase is an attribute of the stubborn disbeliever, then the meaning is that he worships another alongside Allah. We all know that the polytheists used to worship others alongside Allah: they worshipped al-Lat, worshipped al-ʿUzza, worshipped Manat, worshipped Hubal. Each people had an idol they worshipped as they worship Allah; they bowed to it, prostrated to it, loved it as they love Allah, and feared it as they fear Allah. We ask Allah for well-being.

This is if we take ﴿who has set up with Allah another god﴾ as an attribute of this stubborn disbeliever. But if we make it more general, it includes every person who worships other than Allah and humbles himself to other than Allah, even the merchant who has no concern except his trade and its growth; he is a worshipper of it. The evidence for this is that whoever is occupied with something to the point of neglecting obedience to Allah is a worshipper of it. The obstinate disbeliever claims that the companion is the one who led him astray and made him transgress, and the companion denies that.

Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿He will say, "Do not dispute before Me, for I had already sent forth to you the warning.﴾" [Qaf 28]. The disputing is cut off, because the proof is established and there is no excuse for anyone.

﴿And I had already sent forth to you the warning﴾, i.e., I threatened you with punishment for disobedience, so you have no argument.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 50, verse 29:

﴿The word is not changed before Me, and I am not unjust to the servants.﴾ [Qaf 29], meaning: no one can change My word, because judgment belongs to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, alone. So if Allah, exalted is He, has promised or threatened, then He is true to His promise, glorified and exalted is He. As for threats, He may forgive whatever sins He wills, except shirk.

﴿And I am not unjust to the servants﴾, meaning: I do not wrong anyone. Do not say that the word ﴿ẓallām﴾ is an intensive form (sigha mubalagha, intensive form) meaning "I am not one who wrongs much." Rather, it belongs to the category of attribution (nisba), meaning: I am not possessed of injustice. The proof that this is the meaning, and that this meaning is the one that must be intended, is the saying of the Blessed and Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong even an atom's weight; and if it is a good deed, He doubles it﴾ [An-Nisa 40].

And the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer, he will not fear injustice or diminution﴾ [Ta-Ha 112].

And the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾ [Al-Kahf 49].

The verses on this are many: that Allah does not wrong. Indeed, if we reflect, we find that Allah's bounty and beneficence exceed His justice: the recompense for an evil deed is an evil like it, while the recompense for a good deed is ten times its like. Had we intended to apply strict justice, the evil would be repaid with its like and the good with its like, but Allah's bounty exceeds His justice, the Mighty and Majestic. So He, glorified and exalted is He, recompenses with bounty and beneficence the one who does good, and with justice without increase the one who does evil. ﴿The word is not changed before Me, and I am not unjust to the servants﴾. The remainder of the discussion on this surah will come, God willing.

We ask Allah, exalted is He, to benefit us and you by what we have learned, and to make our knowledge a guide for us to His pleasure, for He is capable of all things (...).

We begin, as is our custom, with the tafsir (interpretation) of verses from the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. We are in Surah Qaf, at His saying, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿On the Day when We say to Hell, "Are you filled?" and it says, "Is there any more?"﴾ [Qaf 30]. ﴿Yawma﴾ (on the day) is an adverb of time (ẓarf zamān). Adverbs of time and place, as well as prepositions, must have something they depend on, that is, a verb or something that carries the meaning of a verb.

So what does the phrase ﴿Yawma naqūlu li-Jahannam﴾ depend on? We say it is omitted. The implied meaning is: "Remember the day when We say to Hell..." It should be known that the Arabic language contains words that are omitted, and even whole sentences may be omitted, when the context indicates them. Here, the word on which ﴿yawma﴾ depends is omitted, with the sense: "Remember the day when We say to Hell: Are you filled? and it says: Is there any more?" Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, asks it, "Are you filled?", while He, glorified and exalted, knows whether it has been filled or not, since nothing is hidden from Him. Rather, He asks it ﴿Are you filled?﴾ in order to confirm to it what He, glorified and exalted, promised. Allah says: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind all together."﴾ [Hud 119].

So He asks it, ﴿Are you filled?﴾, meaning: has what Allah promised come to pass? For Allah has undertaken to fill Paradise and to fill the Fire.

Then it says: ﴿Is there any more?﴾. Here ﴿hal﴾ is an interrogative particle, and it is a letter (ḥarf). Is it an interrogative of request (istifhām ṭalab) or an interrogative of negation (istifhām nafy)? Pay attention to the difference. Is it an interrogative of request, meaning that it is asking for more? Or an interrogative of negation, meaning that it is saying: "There is no more beyond what is in me"? On this, the scholars have two opinions. The first opinion: the meaning of ﴿Is there any more?﴾ is "There is no more beyond what is in me," and ﴿hal﴾ comes for the interrogative of negation, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is there any creator other than Allah who provides for you from the heaven and the earth?﴾ [Fatir 3], meaning: there is no creator. Accordingly, the Fire has been filled, since it says: "There is no more beyond that," so the meaning is that it has been filled. It was said, however, that ﴿hal﴾ is for request, meaning that it is asking for more.

When the scholars differ in tafsir or in other matters, the reference is to what Allah and His Messenger have said. So let us look at which of the two opinions is more correct. It is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Hell will not cease to have people cast into it while it says, 'Is there any more?', until the Lord of Might places His foot upon it," or he said, "His leg upon it, and part of it will draw back into part, and it will say: Qat, qat (enough, enough)." [Agreed upon: Bukhari (6661) and Muslim (2848/37), from Anas ibn Malik.]

Which of the two opinions is more correct? It is that the particle is interrogative of request, meaning that it seeks more. But Allah's mercy precedes His wrath. The Mighty and Majestic places His foot upon it in the manner He wills. Then part of it withdraws, part is drawn in towards another part, and it is constricted and says: "There is no more beyond that," or it still seeks more, and then the matter ends. Thus the word of Allah is fulfilled, that He filled Hell with jinn and mankind all together.

In the hadith I have cited there is an affirmation of a foot or leg for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Is it a foot in reality, or is "foot" (qadam) meant as "the one sent forward" (al-muqaddam), meaning that the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, places those whom He sends forward into the Fire until He fills it? And is "leg" (rijl) literal, or is "rijl" meant as a group (ṭā'ifah), since it is said "a rijl of locusts," like "a group of locusts"? Which is more correct? The first: that the intended meaning is a literal leg for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, except that it does not resemble the legs of created beings in any respect. We know with certainty that it is not like the legs of created beings. From where did we know that it is not like the legs of created beings?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, from where did we know that the leg of Allah does not resemble and is not like the legs of created beings?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ [al-Shura 11].

The purpose of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿On the day when We say to Hell﴾, is to warn people, for each one of us does not know whether he will be among the fuel of Hell or among those who are saved from it. We ask Allah to save us and you from it.

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Enter it in peace. That is the Day of Eternity.﴾ [Qaf 34] "Enter it" is a command. Is it a command of obligation (ilzam) or a command of honour (ikram)?

* Students: Honour.

* The Shaykh: It is a command of honour, because in the Hereafter there is no obligation (taklif) or compulsion. Rather, it is either honour or humiliation. As Allah says regarding the criminals: ﴿Enter the gates of Hell﴾ [Az-Zumar 72]; this is a command of humiliation.

His saying regarding the believers here: ﴿Enter it in peace﴾ is a command of honour.

As for His saying: ﴿bi-salam (in peace)﴾, the bā' here is for accompaniment (lil-musahabah). The meaning: entering accompanied by peace. Peace from what? Peace from every affliction. The people of Paradise are free from sicknesses, free from decrepitude, free from death, free from rancour (ghill), free from envy, and free from everything. Everything from which safety is sought, the people of Paradise are safe from it.

﴿Enter it in peace. That﴾, i.e., this day, ﴿is the Day of Eternity (al-khulud)﴾, i.e., the day after which there is no destruction, an everlasting, perpetual eternity with no end.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 50, verse 35:

﴿For them there will be whatever they wish therein﴾ [Qaf: 35], i.e., for these God-fearing people (al-muttaqun), ﴿whatever they wish therein﴾, i.e., in Paradise (al-Jannah), ﴿and with Us there is more﴾, meaning: more than what they wish for and desire. For man, by his nature, is a created being who is unable to exhaust everything, and his wishes come to an end, so that he does not know what he should wish for. But the people of Paradise, whatever they desire therein, it exists.

If a person desires a particular fruit, such as pomegranates or grapes or the like, will he find it? He will find it. At what time? At any time. Everything that a person desires and seeks exists and is not withheld. Rather, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿and with Us there is more﴾, meaning: We will give them beyond what they desire and wish for. And among this increase is the looking upon the Face of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

For this reason, Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, and other scholars, took this verse as evidence for establishing the vision of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and he said: this verse ﴿For them there will be whatever they wish therein, and with Us there is more﴾ is like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿For those who have done good is the best reward and more﴾ [Yunus: 26].

We ask Allah, the Exalted, to make us and you among them, and to grant us the vision of His Noble Face in the Gardens of Bliss.

And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah's blessings and peace be upon our Prophet Muhammad, and upon his family and all his companions.
